n: *Study note:* The antecedent of the pronoun “I” is the angel, not Daniel. The traditional chapter division at this point, and the presence of a chronological note in the verse similar to ones used elsewhere in the book to position Daniel’s activities in relation to imperial affairs, sometimes lead to confusion on this matter.

*Study note:* Perhaps these *three more kings* are Cambyses (ca. 530-522 b.c.), Pseudo-Smerdis (ca. 522 b.c.), and Darius I Hystaspes (ca. 522-486 b.c.).

*Study note:* This *fourth king* is Xerxes I (ca. 486-465 b.c.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rich with great riches.”

*Translator's note:* Or “All [of it] will arouse the kingdom of Greece.” The text is difficult. The text is traditionally taken to have the fourth king as the subject of the verb, making the relationship between הַכֹּל (hakkol, “all, the whole, everyone, everything”) and the kingdom of Greece difficult. Presumably “everyone” is the direct object, but the “kingdom” has the direct object marker אֶת (ʾet). This is very unlikely to be the preposition אֶת (ʾet, “with”) because the verb עוּר (ʿur, “to arouse”) uses the preposition עַל (ʿal) to mean “stir up against.” Nevertheless the meaning “against” is typically supplied or assumed from context. An alternative is to take הַכֹּל as the subject, meaning “all of it,” that is the power and wealth, will arouse [the interest] of the kingdom of Greece. This makes sense of the articular use of הַכֹּל, the parsing of the verb, and the direct object indicator, and also fits the context where in the next verse the Greek king rises up.
*Study note:* The *powerful king* mentioned here is Alexander the Great (ca. 336-323 b.c.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and when he stands.”

*Translator's note:* Or “the heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.

*Study note:* The *king of the south* is Ptolemy I Soter (ca. 323-285 b.c.). The following reference to *one of his subordinates* apparently has in view Seleucus I Nicator (ca. 311-280 b.c.). Throughout the remainder of chap. 11 the expressions “king of the south” and “king of the north” repeatedly occur. It is clear, however, that these terms are being used generically to describe the Ptolemaic king (i.e., “of the south”) or the Seleucid king (i.e., “of the north”) who happens to be in power at any particular time. The specific identity of these kings can be established more or less successfully by a comparison of this chapter with the available extra-biblical records that discuss the history of the intertestamental period. In the following notes the generally accepted identifications are briefly mentioned.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “princes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he”; the referent (the subordinate prince mentioned in the previous clause) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be strong against.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “greater than his kingdom.”

*Study note:* Here *they* refers to Ptolemy II Philadelphus (ca. 285-246 b.c.) and Antiochus II Theos (ca. 262-246 b.c.).

*Study note:* The *daughter* refers to Berenice, who was given in marriage to Antiochus II Theos.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the strength of the arm.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stand,” as also in vv. 7, 8, 11, 13.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his arm.” Some understand this to refer to the descendants of the king of the north.

*Text-critical note:* The present translation reads יַלְדָּה (yaldah, “her child”) rather than the MT יֹלְדָהּ (yoledah, “the one who begot her”). Cf. Theodotion, the Syriac, and the Vulgate.

*Study note:* Antiochus II eventually divorced Berenice and remarried his former wife Laodice, who then poisoned her husband, had Berenice put to death, and installed her own son, Seleucus II Callinicus (ca. 246-227 b.c.), as the Seleucid king.

*Study note:* The reference is to the king of Egypt.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the stock of her roots.”

*Study note:* The reference to *one from her family line* is probably to Berenice’s brother, Ptolemy III Euergetes (ca. 246-221 b.c.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will deal with them and prevail.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew preposition מִן (min) is used here with the verb עָמַד (ʿamad, “to stand”). It probably has a sense of separation (“stand *away from*”), although it may also be understood in an adversative sense (“stand *against*”).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the king of the north) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* The *sons* of Seleucus II Callinicus were Seleucus III Ceraunus (ca. 227-223 b.c.) and Antiochus III the Great (ca. 223-187 b.c.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his”; the referent (the enemy of the king of the north) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he will certainly come and overflow and cross over and return and be aroused unto a fortress.” The translation has attempted to simplify the syntax of this difficult sequence.
*Study note:* This *king of the south* refers to Ptolemy IV Philopator (ca. 221-204 b.c.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his heart will be lifted up.” The referent (the king of the south) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cause to fall.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of myriads.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stand against.”

*Study note:* This was Ptolemy V Epiphanes (ca. 203-181 b.c.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sons of violence.” “Son(s)” is sometimes used idiomatically in Hebrew to indicate that someone is characterized by a certain quality. So the expression “sons of violence” means that these individuals will be characterized by violent deeds.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to cause to stand.”

*Study note:* This *well-fortified city* is apparently Sidon. Its capture from the Ptolemies by Antiochus the Great was a strategic victory for the Seleucid kingdom.

*Translator's note:* Or “choice troops” (BDB 104 s.v. מִבְחָר), or “elite troops” (*HALOT* 542 s.v. מִבְחָר).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he will set his face” (cf. vv. 18, 19).

*Text-critical note:* The present translation reads מֵישָׁרִים (mesharim, “alliances”) for the MT וִישָׁרִים (viysharim, “uprightness”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him”; the referent (the king of the south) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the daughter of the women.”

*Study note:* The *daughter* refers to Cleopatra, the daughter of Antiochus, who was given in marriage to Ptolemy V.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his face,” as also in v. 19.

*Study note:* The *commander* is probably the Roman commander, Lucius Cornelius Scipio.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew here is difficult in that the negative בִּלְתִּי (bilti, “not”) is used in an unusual way. The sense is not entirely clear.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his shameful conduct he will return to him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “on his place.”

*Study note:* The *one who will send out an exactor of tribute* was Seleucus IV Philopator (ca. 187-176 b.c.).

*Study note:* Perhaps this *exactor of tribute* was Heliodorus (cf. 2 Macc 3).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “broken” or “shattered.”
*Study note:* This *despicable person to whom the royal honor has not been rightfully conferred* is Antiochus IV Epiphanes (ca. 175-164 b.c.).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “arms.”

*Text-critical note:* The present translation reads הִשָּׁטֹף (hishatof), Niphal infinitive absolute of שָׁטַף (shataf, “to overflow”), for the MT הַשֶּׁטֶף (hashetef, “flood”).

*Translator's note:* The words “in defeat” are added in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a prince of the covenant.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “broken” or “shattered.”

*Translator's note:* The preposition מִן (min) is probably temporal here (so BDB 583 s.v. 7.c; cf. KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV), although it could also be understood here as indicating means (so J. Goldingay, *Daniel* [WBC], 279, n. 23a; cf. TEV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “nation.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “heart.”

*Study note:* This *king of the south* was Ptolemy Philometer (ca. 181-145 b.c.).
*Text-critical note:* The present translation reads יִשָׁטֵף (yishatef, passive) rather than the MT יִשְׁטוֹף (yishtof, active).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “heart,” as also in v. 28.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “speak.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (the king of the north) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* The name *Kittim* has various designations in extra-biblical literature. It can refer to a location on the island of Cyprus, or more generally to the island itself, or it can be an inclusive term to refer to parts of the Mediterranean world that lay west of the Middle East (e.g., Rome). For *ships of Kittim* the Greek OT (LXX) has “Romans,” an interpretation followed by a few English versions (e.g., TEV). A number of times in the Dead Sea Scrolls the word is used in reference to the Romans. Other English versions are more generic: “[ships] of the western coastlands” (NIV, NLT); “from the west” (NCV, CEV).

*Study note:* This is apparently a reference to the Roman forces, led by Gaius Popilius Laenas, which confronted Antiochus when he came to Egypt and demanded that he withdraw or face the wrath of Rome. Antiochus wisely withdrew from Egypt, albeit in a state of bitter frustration.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “show regard for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “arms.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the sanctuary, the fortress.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will give.”

*Translator's note:* Or “corrupt.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “acted wickedly toward.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “know.” The term “know” sometimes means “to recognize.” In relational contexts it can have the connotation “recognize the authority of, be loyal to,” as it does here.

*Study note:* This is an allusion to the Maccabean revolt, which struggled to bring about Jewish independence in the second century b.c.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the many.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stumble.”

*Translator's note:* Or “by burning.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “days.”

*Study note:* The identity of this king is problematic. If vv. 36-45 continue the description of Antiochus Epiphanes, the account must be viewed as erroneous, since the details do not match what is known of Antiochus’ latter days. Most modern scholars take this view, concluding that this section was written just shortly before the death of Antiochus and that the writer erred on several key points as he tried to predict what would follow the events of his own day. Conservative scholars, however, usually understand the reference to shift at this point to an eschatological figure, *viz*., the Antichrist. The chronological gap that this would presuppose to be in the narrative is not necessarily a problem, since by all accounts there are many chronological gaps throughout the chapter, as the historical figures intended by such expressions as “king of the north” and “king of the south” repeatedly shift.

*Translator's note:* The words “the time of” are added in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “has been done.” The Hebrew verb used here is the perfect of certitude, emphasizing the certainty of fulfillment.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “consider.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the one] desired by women.” The referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “act against.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “for a reward.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “engage in thrusting.”

*Translator's note:* The referent of the pronoun is most likely the king of the south, in which case the text describes the king of the north countering the attack of the king of the south.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “many ships.”

*Translator's note:* This most likely refers to the king of the north who, in response to the aggression of the king of the south, launches an invasion of the southern regions.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and will overflow and pass over.”

*Study note:* The *beautiful land* is a cryptic reference to the land of Israel.

*Translator's note:* This can be understood as “many people” (cf. NRSV) or “many countries” (cf. NASB, NIV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “be delivered from his hand.”

*Translator's note:* Or “Nubians” (NIV84, NCV); *Heb* “Cushites” (NIV11).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Libyans and Cushites [will be] at his footsteps.”
*Study note:* Presumably *seas* refers to the Mediterranean Sea and the Dead Sea.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stands over the sons of your people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will stand up.”

*Translator's note:* Or “from the beginning of a nation.”

*Translator's note:* The words “whose names are” are added in the translation for stylistic reasons and for clarification.
*Study note:* This verse is the only undisputed reference to a literal resurrection found in the Hebrew Bible.

*Study note:* *Many will dash about* is probably an allusion to {{Amos 8:12|Amos 8:12}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “will run back and forth”; KJV “shall run to and fro”; NIV “will go here and there”; CEV “will go everywhere.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one to this edge of the river and one to that edge of the river.”

*Translator's note:* Or “to the heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.

*Text-critical note:* The present translation reads יַד־נֹפֵץ (yad nofets, “hand of one who shatters”) rather than the MT נַפֵּץ־יַד (nappets yad, “to shatter the hand”).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my lord,” a title of polite address.

*Translator's note:* The words “your way” are not in the Hebrew text but are implied.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX lacks “until the end.”

*Translator's note:* The word “receive” is added in the translation for clarification.

*Study note:* The deuterocanonical writings known as the Story of Susanna and Bel and the Dragon appear respectively as chapters 13 and 14 of the book of Daniel in the Greek version of this book. Although these writings are not part of the Hebrew/Aramaic text of Daniel, they were popular among certain early communities who valued traditions about the life of Daniel.
